subject: Quantile dedicated capacity request — token velocity & safety hedge

Subject: Dedicated capacity planning for QNTL-2028-42 — expected token velocity

Hi Tessa,

Thanks for taking this on. We're moving towards a reserved capacity deal and need a concrete GPU sizing recommendation tied to our expected token velocity so we can finalize budget and procurement. High-level expectations:
- Primary model: open-weight custom fine-tune (base: Llama-2-70b) — final artifacts arriving next week
- Typical response size: 150 tokens (median), 95th percentile ~480 tokens
- Avg requests per second (RPS): baseline 300 RPS, peak 1,200 RPS (short bursts up to 2,400 RPS for 10–15m during business hours)
- Mixed workload: 40% short prompts (<=60 tokens), 50% medium (60–200), 10% long (>200)
- SLO target: p95 generation latency <= 650 ms for median/short flows; we can tolerate 1.2s for the longest contexts
- Preferred region: us-west (for latency to our users)

Can you map this to tokens/sec, an estimated GPU count for dedicated slab, and recommended headroom (percent) for safety/bursting? Also flag any assumptions we should surface to procurement. I've attached our QSP light PDF for context.

Olivia
Director of Product, Quantile.ai

Attachment: quantile_qsp.pdf (PDF stub)
From: Tessa Morgan <tessa_morgan@redwood.com>
To: Olivia Park <olivia.park@quantile.ai>
Cc: ben_carter@redwood.com, priyom_das@redwood.com, procurement@quantile.ai
Date: 2028-07-19T11:04:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity planning for QNTL-2028-42 — expected token velocity

Hi Olivia — thanks, this is very helpful. Quick confirmation questions before we bake numbers:
1) Will the fine-tune change average tokens per response materially (we'll assume baseline 150 tokens unless you tell us otherwise).
2) Do you expect a high cache hit rate for repeated system prompts (if yes, effective tokens/sec requirement goes down).

Preliminary sizing (conservative) below — I'm looping in Ben for commercial sizing and Priyom for perf validation. I'm attaching a small workbook (redwood_prelim_sizing_v1.xlsx) with the calc so procurement can see line items.

Summary (high level):
- Calculated steady-state tokens/sec (baseline): 300 RPS * 150 tokens = 45,000 tokens/sec
- Peak sustained tokens/sec (expected during heavy hours): 1,200 RPS * 150 tokens = 180,000 tokens/sec
- Short burst tokens/sec (10–15m): 2,400 RPS * 150 tokens = 360,000 tokens/sec

Perf assumptions (conservative planning numbers we use unless Priyom confirms otherwise):
- Per-GPU capacity (plan): 4,200 tokens/sec for Llama-2-70b (Q4_0 quantized profile on A100-80GB class hardware, warm KV-cache; we use a conservative margin vs lab peak)
- Effective tokens/sec after prefix caching / repeated prompts: assume -28% for workloads with high repetition (we'll default 0% until you confirm cache patterns)

GPU math (conservative, no cache):
- Baseline steady-state: 45,000 / 4,200 = ~10.7 -> 11 GPUs
- Peak sustained: 180,000 / 4,200 = ~42.9 -> 43 GPUs
- Burst lane (10–15m): 360,000 / 4,200 = ~85.7 -> 86 GPUs

Recommended reserved slab and hedge: we advise a two-slab approach:
1) Reserved commit slab sized for sustained peak (43 GPUs) to meet committed SLOs and predictable throughput.
2) A reserved burst buffer (separate burst slab or burst-capacity pool) sized for 40 GPUs to cover repeated 10–15m spikes; we recommend an operational headroom of +25% on total committed capacity to avoid degradation while autoscale warms (so 43 * 1.25 => ~54 GPUs committed).

Put simply: commit 54 GPUs (primary slab) + 40 GPUs burst pool = 94 GPUs available. This balances unit cost predictability and operational safety. Ben — will outline pricing/term options and what a 54-GPU commit looks like vs 75/100 GPU tiers. Priyom — can you confirm per-GPU tokens/sec in our internal perf suite and flag any caveats?

Thanks,
Tessa Morgan
Senior AE, Redwood Inference

Hi all — commercial notes and pricing shapes against Tessa's recommended sizing.

Options (monthly committed GPU-equivalent pricing shown as ballpark; final quote pending pricing tier):
A) Committed conservative slab (54 GPUs) + burst pool on-demand: lower monthly cost, surge usage billed at short-term burst rate.
B) Larger committed slab (90 GPUs) to internalize most bursts: higher monthly commit, better unit pricing (x% discount) and simpler procurement.

Annual commitment vs. 12-month: we can structure a 12/24/36-month rung with increasing discounts; procurement typically prefers a 24-month to lock the burst discount and avoid variable surge bills.

Procurement questions you'll likely get:
- Can we get an SLA for p95 generation latency during sustained load (yes — tied to committed slab and rollout policies).
- Can we cap burst spend (we can add a spend guard and pre-approve a maximum burst dollar amount).

I can put a modeled TCO spreadsheet next (cost vs. commit) once Priyom confirms the perf baseline. Olivia — do you have a preferred procurement cadence (legal PO vs. DocuSign)? We've included a DocuSign link in related_links for a draft term sheet if convenient.

—Ben
Director, Strategic Accounts, Redwood Inference
From: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
To: tessa_morgan@redwood.com, ben_carter@redwood.com, Olivia Park <olivia.park@quantile.ai>
Date: 2028-07-20T14:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity planning for QNTL-2028-42 — perf confirmation and calc details

Tessa / Ben / Olivia — ran this through our internal perf harness against the customer's stated profile (Llama-2-70b base, Q4_0 quantized, 2048 context where applicable). Test notes below.

Lab measurements (warm KV cache, steady stream of mixed-length prompts approximating Quantile distribution):
- Short prompts (<=60 tokens): ~6,100 t/s per A100 (Q4_0, optimized kernels)
- Medium prompts (60–200 tokens): ~4,400 t/s per A100 (amortized per-request overhead + attention cost)
- Long prompts (>200 tokens): ~2,600 t/s per A100 (memory & compute bound)

Weighted aggregate (using Quantile mix 40/50/10, median 150 tokens): composite ~= 4,580 t/s per GPU (lab). To be conservative for on-prem variability and model drift, rounding down => plan for 4,200 t/s per GPU (matches Tessa's assumption).

Detailed burst math (confirming Tessa's numbers):
- Peak sustained: 1,200 RPS * 150 tokens = 180k t/s -> 180,000 / 4,200 = 42.85 -> 43 GPUs
- Short burst (2,400 RPS): 360k t/s -> 360,000 / 4,200 = 85.71 -> 86 GPUs

Operational caveats and mitigations:
1) Cold-starts & KV warm-up: first few minutes of a burst can have 20–40% higher latency; recommend warm-up traffic routing (warm-up pool) or pre-warming a small subset of GPUS during predictable events.
2) Model changes after fine-tune: re-run perf pass on the customer's final artifact — quantization/ops can change throughput by ±15–30%.
3) Tail latency: p99 tail is sensitive to IO and slot scheduling; we recommend p95 SLA commitments only while we iterate on tail mitigation (and maintain a larger burst pool during initial launch).

Suggested final operational plan (concrete):
- Commit slab: 54 GPUs (covers 43 GPUs calculated for peak + 25% safety margin for autoscale warm-up and minor variance).
- Burst pool: 40 GPUs on reserved short-term slots (or pre-negotiated burst discount) — this covers typical bursts and keeps burst cost predictable.
- Tech ops runbook: 10-GPU warm-up lane live during business hours; automated prefix-caching for top-50 repeated prompts (expect ~28% reduction in aggregate tokens/sec if enabled).

I'll add the raw perf logs to the shared drive and tag lines in the sizing workbook. If Quantile can commit to a 24-month term, we can also agree to an annual perf re-benchmark at no charge to re-tune the quantization profile.

-- Priyom
Sr. Applied ML Engineer, Redwood Inference
